papers.title: Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a learner-free swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
papers.abstract: The explore/exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). We show that a minimal foraging swarm approaches its optimum - the ideal-free / Nash allocation of a multi-agent resource-sharing game (an equilibrium, not a return maximum) - with no learner and no reward signal. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; this cascade cycle balances exploration and exploitation and drives foragers toward the ideal free distribution. The swarm attains the shape of this optimum (committed foragers track richness with slope 0.94) but not its exact equilibrium - it stays measurably exploitable - reaching it dynamically (~150 steps) through the coupling of recruitment to movement: remove the coupling and matching collapses (0.94 -> 0.08). The RL sits at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule: no step evaluates payoff (reward-free by construction, though the crowd signal is informationally tied to payoff), and the swarm reaches the allocation without learning it (quality plateaus and re-settles after resources move, no cumulative gain). Against a trained baseline the comparison is two-sided: in an easier, disembodied game a learner is more precise, while in the same embodied environment the reward-free swarm reaches ~65% of a validated oracle ceiling at zero training and leads until trained PPO and centralised-critic (CTDE) learners overtake it (~74-75%, 16 seeds, all above the swarm mean) after ~4,000 of 15,000 training steps - its advantage is in budget, not asymptote. In this one setting we read it not as beating RL but as a strong zero-shot, reward-free operating point: a demonstration that the self-organizing physics of a minimal swarm can carry a collective close to the optimum RL seeks, with none of RL's machinery.

papers.title: Optimal concentration and gradient sensing by perfect monitors
papers.abstract: Cells often estimate chemical concentrations from only a few diffusing molecules, whose stochastic motion limits sensing precision. We consider a perfect monitoring instrument that records the instantaneous molecular density throughout a finite region without perturbing the concentration field or distinguishing molecular identities. The standard Berg-Purcell estimator weights all positions uniformly. Here we derive the optimal spatial weighting within a large class of unbiased estimators for both concentration and gradient sensing. Variance minimization maps to an electrostatic problem. Surprisingly, although the instrument monitors the entire volume, the optimal estimator assigns all weight to its boundary, reducing the uncertainty in both concentration and gradient sensing. We extend the results to arbitrary geometries and spatial dimensions.

papers.title: Distinct weak antisymmetric interactions shape human brain functions as probability fluxes
papers.abstract: The functional computation of the human brain is hypothesized to arise from the collective behaviour of the underlying neural network. A method based on an idea from equilibrium statistical mechanics has been applied to infer the underlying interaction network among the brain regions from whole-brain imaging, but recent studies have challenged the equilibrium assumption. Without equilibrium, how does the human brain encode its function in biased state transitions? Here we show that the probability fluxes, which quantify the irreversibility of state transitions, exhibit unique, task-dependent patterns in spontaneous and task-induced whole-cerebral-cortex activity. We then fit an Ising model with asymmetric interactions and reveal that the symmetric interactions among the brain regions are strong and task-independent, whereas the antisymmetric interactions are weak and task-dependent, and that the fitted model reproduces the observed fluxes for most tasks. Our results indicate that the human brain performs its functional computation by subtly modifying the antisymmetric part of the interactions among the brain regions, offering a new explanation for how a similar interaction network supports diverse brain functions. The method can be applied to the time-series data of other high-dimensional many-body systems to reveal the probability fluxes and infer the underlying interactions among components.

papers.title: Stochastic model of elongation-shortening-switching kinetics of a polymeric filament: Critical slowing down of first-passage and finite-size regularization
papers.abstract: Several filamentous biopolymers exhibit unusual polymerization-depolymerization kinetics where continued elongation (shortening) is possible only in an `active' (`inactive') state while occasional random transition (switching) between the active and inactive states takes place. Here, we present a minimal stochastic model capturing only the key features of random elongation-shortening-switching kinetics of a generic filament. The structure and/or function of the filament ends when its length hits a critical value during its shortening; the time to reach this critical length can be formulated as a first-passage time (FPT) and for its calculation the critical length is treated as an absorbing boundary. Moreover, the lengths of the filaments that inspire our model are constrained to a finite maximum value $\mathcal{N}$; therefore, in our model we impose a reflecting boundary beyond which the filament cannot grow. We determined the distribution of the FPT and derived its first two moments. We identify a critical point where the drift of the tip of the filament vanishes making its movement purely diffusive; at this critical point, in the limit $\mathcal{N} \to \infty$, the fluctuations in the FPT diverges and MFPT becomes infinite indicating `critical slowing down'. Our analytical results will serve as the testing ground for the accuracy of the approximate theoretical results of more realistic models for polymerization-depolymerization kinetics of specific bio-filaments.

papers.title: Hydrodynamics of microalgae in sea spray
papers.abstract: Airborne transmission of biological matter is likely to cause numerous respiratory distress in coastal populations during certain harmful algal blooms. While we know that dissolved algal toxins aerosolize, the contribution of particle-associated toxins is still unknown. The observation of microalgae in the atmosphere suggests that cells or cell debris could be a carrier. Exchange of particulate matter between ocean and atmosphere is driven by sea spray: microplastics and bacteria aerosolize in jet droplets, following the bursting of air bubbles. However, current models for particle capture only consider surface effects, which fail to explain how large microalgal cells (5-50 um) can be entrapped in jet drops (100-800 um). Here, we demonstrate with a variety of species that microalgae are consistently captured in jet drops, and derive a new particle capture model based on the hydrodynamics of the jet. Using the enrichment factor, which measures the increase in concentration in the first jet drop relative to the bulk, we uncover two regimes. The transition between regimes strongly depends on cell size. In addition, we highlight the dynamics of particles within the jet and derive an enrichment model based on hydrodynamics rather than surface considerations. This work widens and generalizes established results on bacterial and microplastic entrapment in jet drops, resolving discrepancies found in the literature. Finally, we demonstrate that sea spray can aerosolize toxic Ostreopsis cf. ovata cells. This reveals a potential particulate pathway for airborne toxicity during harmful algal blooms and raises the question of the relative contribution of particles to that of dissolved toxins.

papers.title: The typical red cell makes too little vacuole material for coalescence to build the large vacuoles of pocked cells
papers.abstract: Red blood cells carrying intracellular vacuoles, called pocked cells, are a sensitive marker of splenic function: about 0.5% of cells in healthy people, 20 to 70% after splenectomy. Vacuoles too small to see are common, and visible ones are thought to grow when small ones merge. We tested that idea with a particle model that resolves the cell's membrane, its contents and every vacuole, and with an inventory of the vacuole volume a cell can make. In tube, shear and vascular flows, a cell's vacuoles met within a second, and, allowed to fuse, ten merged into one to five. Meeting is not what limits growth; material is. At the rate measured after splenectomy, all the vacuoles an average cell makes in its 120-day life fuse into one body 0.6 $\mu$m across, the size healthy cells carry, but 16 times smaller in volume than the 1.5-$\mu$m bodies of patients without a spleen. Taking vacuole size as set at formation, a population model in which vacuoles are made mainly in young cells, and far faster in a small minority that alone makes material for a large one, accounts for the published counts, sizes and age profiles and, on first-hand measurements, favours a splenic clearance that rises several-fold as cells age; letting that minority's vacuoles fuse fits nearly as well. At a model splenic slit, the cell's spare surface decided passage, and a vacuole mattered only when it led. A slit experiment would test whether brief encounters fuse vacuoles.

papers.title: Controlling energy delivery with bistable nanostructures
papers.abstract: Countless biological processes are fueled by energy-rich molecules like ATP and GTP that supply energy with extreme efficiency. However, designing similar energy-delivery schemes from the bottom up, essential for the development of powered nanostructures and other \emph{de novo} machinery, presents a significant challenge: how can an energy-rich structure be stable in solution yet still deliver this energy at precisely the right time? In this paper, we present a purely physical mechanism that solves this challenge, facilitating energy transfer akin to ATP hydrolysis, yet occurring between synthetic nanostructures without any biochemical interactions. This targeted energy delivery is achieved by exploiting a differentiable state-based model to balance the energy profiles that govern the structural transitions in the two nanostructures, creating a coupled relaxation pathway with minimal barriers that facilitates energy delivery. We verify the effectiveness and robustness of this mechanism through Langevin Dynamics simulations, demonstrating that a bath of the high-energy structures can systematically and repeatedly drive the target structure out of equilibrium, enabling it to perform tasks. As the mechanism operates only through explicit physical forces without any biochemistry or internal state variables, our results present generic and far-reaching design principles, setting the stage for the next generation of synthetic nanomachines.

papers.title: Orientational frustration drives enhanced diffusion of anisotropic particles in a liquid labyrinth
papers.abstract: Transport of nanoscale objects in complex, structured environments plays a key role in a wide range of processes, from biomolecular dynamics in extracellular spaces to transport in porous materials such as filters and catalysts. While anomalous diffusion is well established, how particle anisotropy governs transport under geometric constraints remains unclear. Here we use 3D single-particle tracking to investigate the diffusion of stiff one-dimensional carbon nanotubes in a continuous soft matter network of interconnected chambers and constrictions. Transport is anomalous and antipersistent, with strong length dependent confinement and trapping, consistent with obstructed diffusion. Unexpectedly, however, escape from confinement is poorly sensitive to nanotube length as opposed to what would be expected of pore mediated transport. Despite a tenfold length increase and significantly enhanced trapping, escape time increased by only ~1.4. Single-particle orientational tracking reveals the origin of this weak scaling. Indeed, long nanotube, i.e. those with length comparable to the chamber dimensions, dynamically align with constrictions enabling efficient, geometry-assisted escape that offsets increased confinement while shorter nanotubes need to screen the volume to find their escape path. These results uncover an alignment-mediated transport mechanism that decouples confinement strength from escape kinetics, distinct from pore-mediated transport mechanisms, establishing a quantitative framework for anisotropic diffusion in complex environments.

papers.title: Quantifying reticulocyte biomechanics in health and disease
papers.abstract: Red blood cell (RBC) populations are mechanically and morphologically heterogeneous, yet how this heterogeneity governs transport, splenic retention and blood rheology in confinement remains unclear. We combine microchannel experiments with dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) simulations to determine how the morphology, deformability and hydrodynamic interaction of immature RBCs (reticulocytes) shape microconfined flow in acute and chronic mountain sickness. Reticulocyte-rich samples present the three shapes that the maturation literature assigns to successive reticulocyte stages -- multilobular, cup-shaped and near-discocytic -- which we model as R1-R3, each with a membrane shear modulus within the range reported for reticulocytes. A 5-um microchannel resolves these models only weakly, R1 taking at most ~18% longer than control discocytes to cross it, whereas a 1.5-um splenic slit, driven at its own loading, delays R1 by ~30%; both geometries order the models by shear modulus. In cell pairs, a leading cell never lets a follower pass below its own single-cell threshold, ruling out the order-of-magnitude reduction that a wake-"unjamming" picture would suggest; instead the follower queues behind the leader, and a stiffer leader, which clears the slit more slowly, delays it more. The controlling variable is the single-cell critical pressure gradient Delta P_c, which rises monotonically from control discocytes through the reticulocyte subtypes to sickled cells. Set against published rheograms, an analytical estimate attributes chronic-mountain-sickness hyperviscosity mainly to hematocrit-driven crowding rather than single-cell rheology. These results place benign acclimatization, chronic-mountain-sickness hyperviscosity and sickle-cell-trait splenic syndrome on a single mechanical axis defined by Delta P_c.
